newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-HAVELANGE BACKS ARGENTINE TO BE FIFA BOSS.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-HAVELANGE BACKS ARGENTINE TO BE FIFA BOSS.

text.p: World soccer chief Joao Havelange has backed Argentine Julio Grondona as his potential heir.
The 80-year-old Brazilian, due to retire as FIFA president next year, declared open hostilities with Europe with his support for the head of the Argentine Football Association (AFA).
"Julio is a great friend, he's like my brother," Havelange told a news conference in Buenos Aires.
"He's a great leader who may continue along the road I took many years ago if he is elected president of FIFA.
"But before that we must fight, especially against European countries who want to place their candidates at the helm of world football."
UEFA head Lennart Johansson of Sweden has already announced his bid to replace Havelange and is the leading candidate.
FIFA's Swiss general secretary Sepp Blatter has also been tipped as a possible successor while non-European names mentioned include Issa Hayatou of Cameroon.

Havelange has made it quite clear in the past that he does not want Johansson to get the job and soccer insiders say there is a growing body within FIFA concerned about possible future "Europeanisation".
One top non-European FIFA official has reportedly written to Havelange asking him to delay his retirement and stand again at the election in 1998.
But Havelange seems set on leaving the position he has held since 1974 although he had previously refrained from naming his preferred heir.

"I don't think we have ever heard this before, that he would support any particular individual," said UEFA spokesman Frits Ahlstrom of Havelange's ringing endorsement of his old South American friend.
"I think that there will be no comment from UEFA about it. It won't help anybody," he added.
Johannsson was on holiday and not immediately available for comment.
Soccer sources have said in the past that now Havelange has declared his retirement, he has lost much of his power in influencing FIFA decisions.
"I think UEFA's attitude in this would be that we never show surprise or disappointment because we don't expect anything," added Ahlstrom.
However, he did say that he thought it "only natural" for Havelange to back Grondona as an old friend and rejected the assertion that the battle lines were drawn.
"That would be against the attitude of Mr Johansson," he said. "He wants to see FIFA as a family like UEFA.
"He never sees it as a battle between Europe and the rest of the world. We never talks of a battle. We prefer to talk of dialogue and discussion."
FIFA spokesman Andreas Herren said that the world body's general attitude was one of no comment.
Grondona is a FIFA vice-president and was appointed last December as chairman of FIFA's finance committee.
He was the man who, as head of the Argentine association, had the task of announcing at the 1994 World Cup in the United States that the team captain Diego Maradona had failed a dope test. REUTER
